newsitem.title: CUBA: Canada minister, in Cuba, shrugs off U.S. criticism.
newsitem.headline: Canada minister, in Cuba, shrugs off U.S. criticism.

text.p: Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, shrugging off sharp U.S. criticism of the trip, began a visit to Havana on Tuesday that underscored Ottowa's difference with Washington over Cuba policy.
Axworthy, accompanied by Secretary of State for Latin America and Africa Christine Stewart, flew into Havana for the highest-level visit by a Canadian official in two decades.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters Canada was rewarding President Fidel Castro by sending its foreign minister to visit the island and possibly meet the nation's communist leader.
"It doesn't make sense to reward a dictator in our own hemisphere who's completely behind the times," Burns said, reiterating Washington's view Cuba should be isolated.

Asked about Burns's remarks by reporters at Havana airport, Axworthy said he was not aware of the comments, but that the aim of his visit was an exchange of viewpoints with Cuban authorities. He added the U.S. official's comments were not important since "every country has a right to its own foreign policy".
Axworthy was taken on a brief tour of the historic centre of Havana by his Cuban counterpart, Roberto Robaina, before the two sat down for talks at the Foreign Ministry on Tuesday evening.

In public comments before the talks began, Robaina praised Canada for taking a different approach to Cuba from the United States. He told Axworthy that "unlike others, your country has not shared the policy of isolation and blockade on Cuba, which is something we appreciate".

Axworthy, who was scheduled to meet Castro late on Tuesday evening, was likely to put some focus on human rights and governance issues during his 24-hour visit, although he did not specify this in his brief remarks to reporters at the airport.
He said in his comments before the talks with Robaina that while Cuba and Canada did not share the same view on all issues, Ottowa sought a frank and open dialogue.

Canadian officials have stressed that Ottawa seeks to encourage change on the island through dialogue and constructive engagement, rather than trying to force it through isolation, as Washington has done.

But this difference with the United States has been highlighted since Washington toughened its 35-year-old economic embargo on Havana last year with the so-called Helms-Burton law, which includes provisions to punish some third country firms doing business with Cuba. Ottawa has been a leading opponent of the law.

Axworthy is expected to work on a joint declaration for future cooperation on areas including some steps on human rights and governance. Such a public declaration would be a move forward from private discussion of such issues that has taken place recently between Cuban and Canadian officials.
Canadian officials say any such document would be the product of dialogue, adding while Canada wants results, it is not explicitly putting conditions on its ties with Havana.

This puts Canada on a different course from the European Union, which adopted a tougher stance toward Cuba last December, saying increased cooperation with Havana depended on steps towards economic and political reforms in Cuba.

Canadian firms are leading investors in Cuba in sectors such as mining, oil exploration and tourism. Canadians are among the largest group of foreign tourists to Cuba. Bilateral trade was $425 million in 1995 and $400 million in the first 10 months of 1996, according to Canadian officials.

Axworthy's visit, the first by a Canadian Foreign Minister since Castro's 1959 revolution, follows a trip to Canada last October by deputy Cuban president Carlos Lage. The last high-level visit by a Canadian to Cuba was that of former prime minister Pierre Trudeau in 1976.
